title: Permissions
description: Granular control over what Claude Code can do: modes, rules, configuration, and sandboxing.

articles.title: The evaluation pipeline
articles.summary: Before executing any tool, the SDK walks through five steps in order. The first step that resolves the decision wins — the rest aren't evaluated.

blocks.content: Every time Claude wants to use a tool, the SDK evaluates a chain of five decisions. Order matters: a deny rule can block something even if the active mode is `bypassPermissions`.

items.title: Hooks
items.body: Run first. They can approve, deny, or pass the decision to the next step. They can also modify the tool call before it executes. Always run, no exceptions.

items.title: Deny rules
items.body: `disallowed_tools` and the deny rules in `settings.json` are checked. If there's a match, the tool is blocked **even under `bypassPermissions`**. Highest priority.

items.title: Permission mode
items.body: The active mode is applied. `bypassPermissions` approves everything that reaches this point. `acceptEdits` approves file operations. The other modes pass to the next step.

items.title: Allow rules
items.body: `allowed_tools` and the allow rules in `settings.json` are checked. If the tool is listed, it's approved automatically without calling the callback.

items.title: canUseTool callback
items.body: If nothing above resolved the decision, your callback is called for runtime approval. In `dontAsk` mode this step is skipped and the tool is **denied**.

blocks.title: Order matters
blocks.content: Deny rules are evaluated **before** the permission mode. This means you can use `bypassPermissions` while still blocking specific tools with `disallowed_tools` — something `allowed_tools` can't do in that mode.

articles.title: The six permission modes
articles.summary: Each mode defines a global behavior for tools not resolved by hooks, deny rules, or allow rules. It's configured at startup or changed dynamically during streaming.

items.title: default
items.description: Standard mode. Doesn't auto-approve anything. Every tool not resolved by allow rules reaches the `canUseTool` callback. Ideal starting point.

items.title: dontAsk
items.description: Turns any permission prompt into a silent denial. Tools that aren't pre-approved are rejected without calling `canUseTool`. Defines a fixed surface.

items.title: acceptEdits
items.description: Auto-approves all file operations within the working directory. Claude edits code freely. Bash commands and other tools still require approval.

items.title: bypassPermissions
items.description: Approves every tool without prompts. Claude has full system access. Hooks and deny rules remain effective. Only for controlled environments.

items.title: plan
items.description: Completely prevents tool execution. Claude analyzes and creates detailed plans, but makes no changes. `AskUserQuestion` is still available.

items.title: auto
items.description: A model classifier evaluates each tool call and decides whether to approve it. Available in the Agent SDK in both TypeScript and Python. Reduces friction without opening everything up with `bypassPermissions`.

blocks.title: Inheritance in subagents with bypassPermissions
blocks.content: When you use `bypassPermissions`, all subagents inherit this mode and **it cannot be overridden**. Subagents can have different system prompts and less restricted behavior. Enabling it gives them full autonomous access to the system.

articles.title: Allow & Deny rules: declarative control
articles.summary: allowed_tools and disallowed_tools add entries to the approval and denial lists. They don't control which tools exist — they control whether they're auto-approved.

left.label: allowed_tools ✅
items: Listed tools are auto-approved without going through `canUseTool`
Unlisted ones still fall through to the permission mode and the callback
Doesn't restrict `bypassPermissions` — unlisted tools are still approved in that mode
Use it together with `dontAsk` for a minimal surface

right.label: disallowed_tools 🚫
items: Listed tools are **always** denied
Takes priority over any mode, including `bypassPermissions`
It's the only way to guarantee a tool never runs
A bare deny (`Bash`) hides the tool from Claude's context

blocks.title: Common trap
blocks.content: `allowedTools: ["Read"]` together with `permissionMode: "bypassPermissions"` **restricts nothing**. Unlisted tools aren't denied — they still fall through to the mode, where `bypassPermissions` approves all of them. For a minimal surface, use `dontAsk` + `allowedTools`, not `bypassPermissions` + `allowedTools`.

blocks.label: Recommended combinations
.claude/settings.json — declarative per-project rules

articles.title: Dynamic mode switching
articles.summary: You can change the permission mode while streaming is active. The new mode takes effect immediately. This enables progressive-trust patterns.

items.title: Start restrictive
items.body: Begin with `plan` or `default`. Claude analyzes the code and proposes what it would change. You review the plan before anything executes.

items.title: Evaluate the proposal
items.body: If the plan looks good and the changes are within the expected scope, you call `setPermissionMode("acceptEdits")` so it proceeds with the edits.

items.title: Escalate if needed
items.body: If the agent needs system commands in addition to editing files, you can escalate to `bypassPermissions` right at that point — in an isolated environment where you trust the operations.

items.title: Lock down if something goes out of scope
items.body: You can go back to `dontAsk` to cut off access immediately if the agent attempts something outside what was expected.

blocks.label: Python — progressive trust
blocks.content:
async def main():
    q = query(
        prompt="Refactor the auth module",
        options=ClaudeAgentOptions(
            permission_mode="plan",  # starts without execution
        ),
    )
    # Claude analyzes and proposes — you review the plan
    await q.set_permission_mode("acceptEdits")  # ok, let it edit
    async for message in q:
        if hasattr(message, "result"):
            print(message.result)

blocks.label: TypeScript — progressive trust

blocks.title: The most effective pattern
blocks.content: Start with `plan` for complex or high-impact tasks. Once the plan convinces you, switch dynamically to `acceptEdits` or `default` so it executes. You get the best of both worlds: thoroughness while planning, speed while executing.

articles.title: How Claude thinks depending on the mode
articles.summary: Each mode doesn't just change which tools Claude can use — it changes its reasoning strategy. This dimension is less obvious but just as important.

left.label: default — act to understand
items: Has a safety net: can run intermediate steps and correct course
Acts incrementally without needing much prior context
Opens the file, reads, edits, corrects along the way
Context builds up as it goes

right.label: plan — understand to act
items: The plan is the final product — can't fix mistakes by running more steps
Explores, seeks additional context, asks questions before committing
Proposes the complete plan at once, with all the necessary changes
More thorough in the upfront analysis

blocks.title: The analogy
blocks.content:
**default** = the agile developer: starts coding, hits an error, fixes it, moves on. If something goes wrong, there's a `git reset`.

**plan** = the surgeon: studies the X-rays, reviews the history, and plans every incision before touching the patient. No room to improvise in the operating room.

rows: Acts incrementally. Uses execution as feedback to correct course.
Designs the approach around the tools available. Doesn't attempt what it knows is blocked.
Flows through code edits, but pauses when it needs to leave the filesystem. Prefers edit-based solutions.
More direct decisions, chains operations without interruptions. Maximum efficiency, minimum caution.
Explores before committing. The plan is the final product — needs to be confident before proposing it.
Proposes granular, well-justified operations, because each one goes through independent classifier evaluation.

blocks.title: When does each strategy make sense?

items.title: Use default when…
items.description: The task is concrete and bounded, you can supervise the changes as they happen, and you're in a repo with git — mistakes are reversible.

items.title: Use plan when…
items.description: You want to review the scope before anything is touched, the task affects many files, or the changes are hard or costly to revert.

items.title: Use dontAsk when…
items.description: You have a headless agent with predefined tools and want zero human intervention at runtime.

items.title: Use acceptEdits when…
items.description: You're prototyping quickly in an isolated directory and trust Claude's edits, but want oversight for system commands.

articles.title: Advanced syntax and trap cases
articles.summary: Tool specifiers let you approve or block specific invocations, not just entire tools. The interaction between tools creates non-obvious scenarios.

blocks.label: Base specifier syntax
Glob patterns for Bash — * matches spaces too

blocks.title: Safety with shell operators
blocks.content: Claude Code understands `&&`, `||`, `;`, `|`, `|&`, `&`, and newlines — and evaluates each subcommand separately. A `Bash(safe-cmd *)` rule doesn't give it permission to run `safe-cmd && evil-cmd`. Claude Code parses the full command, splits it into subcommands, and evaluates each part independently. If any subcommand lacks permission, the entire compound command is blocked.

blocks.label: Paths for Read and Edit — prefixes and anchor points

rows: `cat .env` run from Bash doesn't use the Read tool
Bash can use `curl` or `wget` to reach any URL
Unlisted tools aren't denied — bypass approves all of them
Claude doesn't see the tool in its context — it can't even propose it
Use `deny: ["Bash(rm *)"]` if you only want to block specific commands

articles.title: Configuration in settings.json
articles.summary: Rules are defined declaratively in .claude/settings.json and apply to the whole project. There are five precedence levels — deny always wins across levels.

blocks.label: .claude/settings.json — full configuration
Read-only agent — can explore, never modify
Controlling MCP servers and subagents

items.title: Managed settings
items.body: MDM / server-managed. Cannot be overridden by any other level. If a tool is denied here, nothing can allow it.

items.title: Command line args
items.body: `--allowedTools` / `--disallowedTools`. Temporary per-session overrides. Take precedence over any settings.json.

items.title: Local project settings
items.body: `.claude/settings.local.json` — not committed. For personal overrides you don't want to share with the team.

items.title: Shared project settings
items.body: `.claude/settings.json` — committed. The team's rules that apply to every developer on the project.

items.title: User settings
items.body: `~/.claude/settings.json` — global for the user. Applies to every project. Useful for personal cross-project rules.

blocks.title: Cross-level deny
blocks.content: If `user settings` has a deny and `project settings` has an allow for the same tool, **deny wins**. It doesn't matter which one is "higher" in the hierarchy — a deny rule from any level blocks the tool. Only managed settings can ignore rules from lower levels with `allowManagedPermissionRulesOnly: true`.

blocks.title: Pre-approved Bash commands (read-only built-in)
blocks.content: Claude Code has a built-in list of commands that run without a prompt in any mode: `ls`, `cat`, `echo`, `pwd`, `head`, `tail`, `grep`, `find`, `wc`, `which`, `diff`, `stat`, `du`, `cd`, plus the read-only forms of `git` (the official documentation doesn't enumerate every one — `git log`, `git status`, and `git diff` are examples, but there are more like `git show`). You don't need to list them in `allowedTools`. If you want to block one, explicitly add `deny: ["Bash(cat *)"]`.

articles.title: Sandboxing
articles.summary: Sandboxing sits one level below permissions: it restricts at the OS level what Bash commands can touch — filesystem and network — regardless of which tools are allowed.

left.label: Without sandboxing ❌
items: Every Bash command requires manual approval
Approval fatigue: repeated clicking without reading carefully
Claude can't work autonomously
Prompt injection can exfiltrate data

right.label: With sandboxing ✅
items: Limits defined up front, fewer prompts
Claude works freely within the sandbox
Applies to every subprocess: kubectl, npm, terraform…
Immediate notification if something tries to escape the boundary

blocks.title: Effective sandboxing requires both layers
blocks.content: Without network isolation, a compromised agent can exfiltrate sensitive files like SSH keys. Without filesystem isolation, it can backdoor system resources to gain network access. The two restrictions complement each other — configuring only one leaves gaps.

blocks.label: Enabling sandboxing
blocks.content:
# From a Claude Code session
/sandbox

# Or in settings.json
# "sandbox": { "enabled": true }

blocks.label: Full sandbox configuration

blocks.title: Tools that require excludedCommands
blocks.content: **docker** — accesses the host's Docker socket, which the sandbox blocks. **watchman** — incompatible with the sandbox; if you use Jest, consider `jest --no-watchman`. **WSL2 + Windows bins** — `cmd.exe`, `powershell.exe`, and binaries under `/mnt/c/` can't be launched from the sandbox in WSL2.

left.label: Permissions
items: Control which tools Claude can use
Evaluated before any tool runs
Apply to every tool: Bash, Read, Edit, WebFetch, MCP

right.label: Sandboxing
items: Control what each command can touch at the OS level
Enforced afterward, at the kernel level
Only applies to Bash and its subprocesses

articles.title: CI/CD: non-interactive mode without hangs or unsafe bypass
articles.summary: Invoking Claude Code in a pipeline without first resolving interactivity produces jobs that hang waiting for an approval no one can give — and the most common reaction, skipping permissions entirely, trades that problem for a worse one.

blocks.content: A pipeline that invokes Claude Code as if it were an interactive terminal session, without `-p`/`--print`, hangs on the first tool call that requires confirmation — there's no one on the job's side to respond to the prompt, and the step ends up failing on a timeout, intermittently depending on which action triggers the confirmation on each run. The reflex reaction is usually to add `--dangerously-skip-permissions`: the hang disappears, but so does any gate over destructive commands, right in the environment — CI — that typically has access to deployment credentials and registry tokens.

left.label: --dangerously-skip-permissions without a sandbox ❌
items: Resolves the hang, but removes every approval gate
Any command the model decides to run executes unchecked
The CI environment usually has access to deployment secrets
No trace of what was approved and what wasn't — everything is approved

right.label: --print + dontAsk + versioned allowlist ✅
items: `-p`/`--print` runs in and out without prompts; with `--output-format json` the output integrates structurally into the pipeline
`--permission-mode dontAsk` auto-denies anything not pre-approved, instead of waiting for a response
The allowed surface lives in `.claude/settings.json`, versioned and reviewable in code review
`--bare` skips loading hooks, skills, or CLAUDE.md from the local machine — the same run on any runner

blocks.label: Correct invocation in a pipeline
blocks.content:
claude --bare -p "Review the diff and fix the lint failures" \
  --output-format json \
  --permission-mode dontAsk \
  --settings .claude/settings.json

blocks.title: Bypass isn't the solution, it's a different problem
blocks.content: `--dangerously-skip-permissions` can make sense inside an ephemeral, isolated container with no production credentials mounted — never as a generic answer to a permission prompt hanging. If the pipeline needs a specific operation to run without friction, that operation gets added to `allow` in `settings.json`; the entire permission system doesn't get switched off to avoid configuring one rule.
